samehost matches the server's own IP addresses, and samenet matches addresses in directly connected subnets. When a host name is used, PostgreSQL first checks reverse resolution of the client IP to a host name, then does a forward lookup of that host name to confirm the client address.

**peer authentication** is available **only for local connections** (Unix-domain sockets); it obtains the client's OS user name from the kernel and maps it to a PostgreSQL role via pg_ident.conf.

**ident authentication** is available **only for TCP/IP connections**; it uses the IDENT protocol (RFC 1413) to look up the OS user from an external ident service (typically port 113) and maps it to a PostgreSQL role via pg_ident.conf. If ident is specified for a local connection, PostgreSQL uses peer instead.

The key difference is the connection type (local vs. TCP/IP) and the source of the OS user name (kernel vs. external ident service). peer is generally more secure than ident because it does not rely on an external, potentially spoofable service.

PostgreSQL supports RANGE, LIST, and HASH partitioning. RANGE and LIST partitioning benefit most from partition pruning (skipping irrelevant partitions when the WHERE clause filters on the partition key), while HASH partitioning does not benefit from pruning because each row maps to a fixed bucket regardless of query pattern.

A role with LOGIN can connect to the database (acts as a user), while a role without LOGIN cannot connect directly and is used as a group to which other roles are granted membership via GRANT role1 TO role2.

SET ROLE allows a role to assume the privileges of another role it is a member of; session_user remains the original login role while current_user changes to the assumed role and is reset with SET ROLE NONE.

pg_basebackup creates a binary copy of the entire running database cluster via the streaming replication protocol (output as tar with -Ft or plain directory; use -X stream to include WAL), and is the foundation for setting up a new standby server; pg_dump produces a logical backup of a single database as a SQL script or custom-format archive (parallel/selective restore via pg_restore), is online (does not block reads or writes), and is the standard tool for migrations and small-to-medium backups.
